modes.label: Never surfaced in reasoning
modes.description: The requirement appears nowhere in the reasoning trace or the answer — it was never extracted from the prompt into the model's working plan (e.g., a formatting sub-rule the planning checklist skips entirely).
strategy: The leading named method is RLCF — Reinforcement Learning from Checklist Feedback (CMU + Apple, NeurIPS 2025) — which extracts an instruction-specific checklist from each prompt, scores candidate responses per checklist item using both AI judges and specialized verifier programs, and combines the per-item scores into an RL reward. Applied to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, RLCF was the only tested method to improve performance on every benchmark, including a 4-point hard-satisfaction gain on FollowBench and a 6-point gain on InFoBench — evidence that checklist-shaped, per-instruction rewards, rather than a single fixed-criteria reward model, are what teach a model to enumerate every requirement instead of silently skipping some. RLCF is CMU+Apple academic/applied research, not a disclosed frontier-lab production method, and its published training pipeline is compute-heavy (about four days on 8xH100 GPUs for 130K instructions), so a commissioning lab should expect meaningful compute overhead alongside the data spend.

RECAST (also published as RLVC) is a second, independent instantiation of the same idea: constraints are extracted from real-world prompt-response pairs rather than invented templates, and each training instance carries its full constraint set plus a per-constraint validation method, feeding a GRPO reward with an independent reward channel per constraint. RECAST is a preprint without a confirmed peer-review venue, so its reported gains should be treated as medium-confidence. At inference time, DeCRIM (Amazon, Findings of EMNLP 2024) complements both training-time methods: it decomposes an instruction into a constraint checklist and loops Critique-Refine until every constraint passes, improving Mistral's RealInstruct and IFEval scores by 7-8 points even under weak feedback, and letting open-source Mistral surpass GPT-4 on both benchmarks under oracle feedback.

What unifies all three methods is that they attack the extraction step directly: none assumes the model already knows the constraint exists — each forces explicit checklist construction before scoring or refining a response, which is exactly the missing step in this failure mode. A lab commissioning data for constraint_never_surfaced should therefore prioritize exhaustive requirement-enumeration supervision, checklist-style SFT and reward, over generic instruction-following fine-tuning, since the failure is one of omission at the planning stage rather than misapplication at the answer stage.

modes.label: Tracked in reasoning, lost from answer
modes.description: The trace tracks or even verifies the requirement, but iterative replanning, patchwork corrections, or final transcription loses it — the answer omits or contradicts what the trace established.
strategy: Counterfactual Simulation Training (CST) (Hase & Potts, Feb 2026) is the strongest verified method lead for CoT-to-answer faithfulness — training a model so that constraints tracked in its reasoning actually govern its output. CST rewards CoTs that let a simulator accurately predict the model's outputs over counterfactual inputs; in experiments up to 235B parameters it substantially improved monitor accuracy on cue-based counterfactuals (by 35 accuracy points) and simulatability over generic counterfactuals (by 2 points). It is a two-author, non-peer-reviewed preprint, not a disclosed frontier-lab production method; gains did not generalize from persuading to dissuading cues, and the generic-counterfactual gain is modest, so treat it as a promising but early-stage lever rather than a proven production recipe.

Conifer supplies a concrete process-feedback annotation format directly usable for constraint-retention training: internal feedback, where GPT-4 explicitly demonstrates constraint adherence inside its own responses (scoped to format/numerical constraints), and external feedback, where GPT-4 identifies constraints it failed to adhere to in the most challenging cases and uses that judgement to construct a corrected multi-turn conversation in the form {Difficult Instruction, Model Response, GPT-4 Judgement, GPT-4 Response}. Conifer's paper targets constraint failures generally rather than specifically the reasoning-trace-to-final-answer drop this mode names, so the mapping to this mode is interpretive rather than a direct claim of the source.

A third, complementary lever is training a dedicated constraint-tracking critic: Mistral v0.2, LoRA-fine-tuned on GPT-4-Turbo CoT reasoning trails annotating constraint satisfaction over RealInstruct's validation split, gains +12.9 Macro F1 and +28.1 F1-Negative on constraint verification, and plugging this Supervised Critic into DeCRIM lifts Mistral +3.7 points on RealInstruct — while pure self-critique (Self-Refine) yields only marginal gains or degrades IFEval. This is direct evidence that trained, externally sourced feedback substantially outperforms unstructured self-correction for catching constraints a trace already established but the answer later dropped.

Across all three levers, the realistic commission is judge/rubric-dependent throughout: GPT-4 identifies constraint failures and writes corrections (Conifer), or a critic model is trained on GPT-4-Turbo-annotated satisfaction labels (RealInstruct's critic data). No verified method here runs a rule-based verifier end to end, so a lab commissioning constraint_dropped data should budget for LLM-judge-in-the-loop annotation rather than expect an RLVR shortcut.

modes.label: Noticed, then overridden
modes.description: The trace names the constraint, then argues itself out of honoring it — habit, source-material conventions, helpfulness instincts, or a self-invented reinterpretation wins over the explicit instruction.
strategy: OpenAI's published lineage on this mode is the clearest multi-year trajectory in the material, running from the instruction hierarchy (Wallace et al., Apr 2024) through deliberative alignment (Dec 2024) to IH-Challenge (~Mar 2026), moving from judge-graded to fully auto-verifiable reward design as the method matures. The instruction hierarchy establishes an explicit priority ordering (system > user > tool) plus a data-generation method teaching models to selectively ignore lower-privileged instructions on conflict: context-synthesis data for aligned requests, and context-ignorance data whose target label is the same answer the model would have generated had it never seen the lower-privileged instruction, with 'ignore' as ideal behavior and 'refuse' as fallback. Labels here are behavioral targets, not preference pairs, generated synthetically via self-distillation, and verifying compliance requires human/model judgment of semantic equivalence — not auto-verifiable. It shipped in GPT-4o mini and fed the Model Spec's chain of command.

Deliberative alignment teaches the model the literal text of safety/policy specifications and trains it to explicitly recall and reason over them in the CoT before answering, used to align the o-series. Its SFT data is synthesized by prompting a base reasoning model with the spec text so the CoT cites the spec, filtered by a spec-conditioned judge, then the spec is stripped from the training prompt; the RL reward on safety-relevant prompts reuses a judge model with access to the safety policies — rubric/spec-conditioned model-graded reward, requiring no human-labeled completions and no rule-based verifier.

IH-Challenge is OpenAI's newest published strategy: RL on a 27,570-row instruction-hierarchy dataset requiring each task to be objectively gradable by a per-datapoint Python grader that stays valid under adversarially synthesized instruction conflicts, explicitly to resist reward hacking from LLM judges. Fine-tuning GPT-5-Mini with online adversarial example generation raised average instruction-hierarchy robustness across 16 benchmarks from 84.1% to 94.1% and cut unsafe behavior from 6.6% to 0.7% — this dataset is fully RLVR-ready by design. Outside OpenAI, VerIH independently reframes instruction-hierarchy resolution as a reasoning task trained with lightweight RLVR, raising Qwen3-8B's conflict-set performance on IHEval from 46.48% to 63.48% while preserving aligned-set performance, with the effect transferring out-of-distribution to safety metrics — evidence the RLVR-for-hierarchy pattern reproduces outside OpenAI's own pipeline, though VerIH is academic research, not a confirmed frontier-lab production method.

This mode shows the clearest evidence of maturing from judge-dependent to RLVR-ready: a lab commissioning data today for objective, format-style conflicts should specify per-datapoint verifiable graders in the IH-Challenge/VerIH pattern, while genuinely subjective hierarchy conflicts (e.g. jailbreak nuance) still require LLM judges — which is why IH-Challenge itself restricts its dataset to objectively gradable tasks rather than claiming full coverage.

modes.label: Sacrificed to a competing constraint
modes.description: Under real or perceived conflict (coverage vs ceilings, word caps vs completeness, time budget vs task list), the model satisfies one requirement by violating another — often asserting compliance anyway instead of surfacing the tradeoff.
strategy: OpenAI's 'confession' training is the most direct verified method for this mode: RL on top of GPT-5-Thinking where, following a post-answer system request, the model produces a structured self-report of its own compliance (a ConfessionReport), with the confession's reward graded solely on honesty by an LLM judge and firewalled from the main task reward — directly targeting silent constraint trade-offs and compliance overclaiming. When the model misbehaves it confesses at least half the time in 11 of 12 out-of-distribution evaluations spanning instruction following, instruction hierarchy, hallucination, scheming, and reward hacking, with a 74.3% average probability of confessing conditioned on bad behavior. Confessions work best for knowing, intentional violations and fail mostly on unintentional errors, so OpenAI itself positions the method primarily as a deployment monitoring/diagnostic tool rather than the primary training signal.

CoCoNot broadens the strategy to noncompliance and infeasibility more generally, benchmarking mitigation strategies including continued SFT (LoRA) on its noncompliance set and DPO on its contrast set, where compliant responses are preferred over noncompliant ones for benign look-alike queries. Even GPT-4 incorrectly complies with as many as 30% of requests in previously understudied noncompliance categories, per CoCoNot's own evaluation suite.

A separate 2026 compliance-gap study is a diagnostic benchmark rather than a training method, but it pinpoints exactly which constraint types this mode needs new reward designs for: across default-framing sessions, all six tested frontier models showed 0% actual compliance with user-issued process instructions while verbally agreeing to follow them, and non-compliance tracked the RLHF reward gradient rather than user instructions — models complied 97% of the time on tasks where rationale is rewarded versus 0-4% where it is not. Removing delegation tools raised compliance from 0% to 74.7%, and a single in-session correction prompt achieved 100% repair, telling a commissioning lab which constraint types are training-signal gaps versus prompt-level fixes.

HIPO formulates hierarchical instruction following as a constrained Markov decision process, training with primal-dual safe RL plus a GRPO-style policy gradient on deliberately mixed compliant and conflicting data, with reward from a dual LLM-as-judge protocol scoring system- and user-compliance separately. On the conflicting test split HIPO raises Qwen3-1.7B system-prompt compliance to threshold while plain SFT's compliance stays below it — evidence SFT/DPO alone do not internalize hierarchical priority under genuine conflict. Across all four methods this mode is fundamentally judge-dependent, with VerIH's conflict-labeled half a partial exception since its output constraints stay rule-verifiable even though the conflict framing itself is synthetically generated; a commissioning lab should expect to buy judge/rubric infrastructure, not an RLVR shortcut.

modes.label: Constraint misread
modes.description: The requirement is engaged with but interpreted wrongly — scope, boundary semantics ('every week after', 'even if zero'), conditional triggers, or format words ('brackets', 'beside') resolved to the wrong reading.
strategy: HedgeTriple is a named contrastive-training approach purpose-built for negation and hedging semantics: distilled from GPT-3.5 grounded in a linguistic taxonomy of negation (verbal, absolute, affixal, lexical) and a two-type hedging taxonomy (single-word vs. multi-word cues, seeded from HedgePeer). Contrastive fine-tuning of an encoder on HedgeTriple, using Multiple Negative Ranking Loss with hedged sentences as positives and negated sentences as hard negatives, raises NevIR from 8.10 to 40.56 and a 4-benchmark negation average from 32.13 to 54.17, while a 56-dataset MTEB general-capability average moves only from 58.79 to 57.14. Taxonomy-driven pattern diversity beats raw data quantity: HedgeTriple-trained models outperform baselines trained on larger but less diverse negation-only corpora, the design lesson being diversity of negation type over volume. The same data transfers to decoder-only LLMs with a measurable tradeoff: LoRA fine-tuning on HedgeTriple raises the negation-benchmark average from 66.85 to 77.17, while GSM8K drops from 75.36 to 67.10, concentrated in MMLU math subsets — a real capability tradeoff to flag when commissioning this data.

AMBROSIA targets scope, attachment, and vagueness ambiguity with paired unambiguous readings rather than negation specifically. Its headline result — the best model, Llama 3-70B, achieves only 31% recall on ambiguous questions compared to 66% on unambiguous ones — shows models typically commit to a single reading rather than covering all valid interpretations of a scope, attachment, or vague instruction, which is this failure mode operating at the semantic-ambiguity level.

NoFEVER/NoSNLI supplies a third, complementary minimal-pair design for entailment-level negation robustness: paired evaluation sentences differ only in negation of the primary verb, so if one follows from the premise the other contradicts it, making the entailment label logically auto-verifiable given the non-negated label. This paper is evaluation-only and proposes no training method. RECAST's independent-reward-channel design, whose primary home is constraint_never_surfaced, is worth citing here too: it provides an independent reward channel for each constraint and combines verifiable constraints as reward signals with GRPO — evidence that per-constraint verifiable rewards generalize beyond format-style constraints to semantic-type constraints like negation and scope, though RECAST itself is not scoped to negation/ambiguity specifically.

This mode splits into three distinct commissioning postures: fully auto-generatable minimal pairs with no human step (HedgeTriple), human-written ambiguous-reading pairs with execution-based verification (AMBROSIA), and rule-generated-then-fully-human-verified triplets (NoFEVER/NoSNLI). All three land as RLVR-ready at the evaluation stage even where the generation step used humans, so a lab should pick the posture based on whether it needs semantic-ambiguity coverage (AMBROSIA-style, needing human interpretation writing) or negation/hedging robustness (HedgeTriple/NoFEVER-style, largely automatable).

modes.label: Source data misread
modes.description: The failure originates in parsing the prompt's source material: column misalignment, false equivalences between sections, ambiguity silently resolved in the wrong direction.
strategy: The clearest method-level finding here is negative: a controlled table-SFT replication study — the first cross-model, cross-dataset replication for table LLMs, spanning 4 existing table SFT corpora across 3 base models evaluated on 16 table benchmarks — finds a Shapley R-squared decomposition attributing 81.6% of downstream table-task performance variance to base-model choice and only 13.8% to the instruction-tuning dataset. An error analysis of 1,000 predictions from a table-tuned model found grounding errors (wrong column/cell association, this failure mode directly) were the most frequent error type at 67%, far ahead of math reasoning, instruction-following, hallucination, and commonsense errors combined. Narrowly scoped table SFT can actively degrade out-of-domain performance relative to the untuned base model, and best out-of-domain scores fall well below in-domain scores, evidence of overfitting to dataset-specific patterns. The one positive design lesson: the training data built using GPT-3.5 to enrich reasoning traces in training examples consistently produced the best out-of-domain performance across all three base models — reasoning-trace-enriched annotation, not scale, is what generalizes.

TableDreamer is a positive method lead: a progressive, weakness-guided data synthesis framework that improves Llama3.1-8B-Instruct average accuracy across 10 tabular benchmarks by 11.62 points (49.07% to 60.69%) using only 27K GPT-4o-synthesized examples, outperforming data-synthesis baselines that use far more training data — evidence that targeted, weakness-diagnosed synthesis beats generic scale.

ToRR is the diagnostic benchmark establishing input_misread as a real, unsolved capability gap: across 14 leading LLMs from 7 model families, overall table-task performance tops out at 0.50, with wide per-example variance across semantically equivalent table formats, because current models lack a stable, generalizable table representation that persists across formats. No single serialization format (JSON, HTML, CSV, Markdown) consistently wins, implying robustness training data should span multiple serializations rather than standardize on one canonical format.

Input_misread data is mostly auto-generatable and auto-verifiable — TableDreamer's synthesis pipeline and ToRR's execution-based metrics for QA, verification, and classification tasks both require no human labeling step — but ToRR's plateau at 0.50 despite that verifiability shows this is a genuine capability gap, not a labeling gap. Per the replication study, a lab should commission diversity of serialization and perturbation coverage, plus reasoning-trace-enriched annotation, over raw scale, since base-model quality otherwise dominates the outcome regardless of dataset size.

modes.label: Right intent, wrong execution
modes.description: The plan is right but the rendering fails: arithmetic/counting errors, format markup omitted, per-item rules replaced by one template, placeholders never resolved, output never cross-checked against its own derived values.
strategy: VerIF / VerInstruct (THU-KEG, EMNLP 2025) is the clearest RLVR method lead: a verification method combining rule-based code verification with LLM-based verification from a large reasoning model (e.g., QwQ-32B) — rule-based code checks hard, programmatically checkable constraints such as length, format, and keyword usage, while the reasoning-model verifier scores soft constraints, and the GRPO reward averages the 0/1 hard and soft scores. Tulu 3's RLVR stage corroborates the direction at a coarser grain: RLVR at 8B improved GSM8K from 84.3 to 87.6, MATH from 42.0 to 43.7, and IFEval from 81.1 to 82.4 over the DPO starting point.

The same hybrid pattern recurs independently in RLCF, reused from constraint_never_surfaced: specialized verifier programs are generated only for requirements that are explicitly about syntax or format, with everything else judge-graded — a second system landing on the same split between deterministic and judge-graded reward.

Despite the 'RLVR' branding attached to this mode, the data a lab would actually commission is majority judge-graded at the constraint level. VerInstruct's own numbers make this explicit: only about 22.3% of its ~22,000 instances' constraints have deterministic code verifiers, with roughly 77.7% tagged for LLM verification during RL — in other words, even a purpose-built 'RLVR' instruction-following dataset is roughly three-quarters judge-dependent at the constraint level. RECAST's parallel ratio (reused from constraint_never_surfaced) lands close to the same split, at roughly 36% deterministic and 64% judge-graded constraints, feeding a GRPO reward that further improves performance beyond SFT.

A vendor engagement for execution_slip should budget for LLM-judge infrastructure, or a large reasoning model used as a verifier as VerIF does with QwQ-32B, rather than assume a pure programmatic reward pipeline; only the format/length/keyword-style slice of constraints is cheaply auto-verifiable, while arithmetic self-checks and per-item rule adherence largely require judge or reasoning-model scoring to reward correctly.

modes.label: Degenerate generation
modes.description: The generation collapses — repetition loops, endless self-correction, no committed final answer — so whole constraint blocks go unmet at once.
strategy: An overthinking survey names and taxonomizes this failure mode directly: the 'overthinking phenomenon' in large reasoning models, where longer chain-of-thought sequences improve performance but produce verbose, redundant outputs with significant computational overhead. The survey's mitigation taxonomy has three branches — model-based efficient reasoning, reasoning output-based reduction, and input prompt-based enhancement — and within the model-based branch it names a concrete family of training strategies under 'RL with Length Reward Design' (rewarding shorter correct reasoning), cataloging methods including O1-Pruner, L1, DAST, Kimi k1.5, LASER, BRPO, GRPO-lambda, AutoThink, and DeGRPO. The survey is explicit this is a correctness problem, not merely a cost problem: excessive reasoning steps can introduce errors, obscure logical clarity, and prevent answers within a user-defined token budget, supporting treating endless self-correction and no-committed-answer as a genuine training-relevant failure mode.

A separate repetition-loop mechanism paper supplies a causal account of why loops happen: it attributes reasoning-model repetition loops to errors in learning — when the correct progress-making action is hard to learn but an easy cyclic alternative exists, the model shifts probability mass onto the cyclic action, producing loops at low temperature. This has a direct implication for which models need mitigation most: distilled student models loop far more than their teachers (one distilled 1.5B model loops in about 30% of greedy-decoded responses while its 32B teacher barely loops at all), and smaller models loop more than larger ones within a family (a separate distilled model family shows roughly 76%, 51%, and 40% loop rates at its 1.5B, 7B, and 32B sizes, all at temperature zero).

Tulu 3's PPO recipe includes an explicit, shippable termination-commitment reward: any sampled response that fails to emit an end-of-sequence token within the max-token budget receives a fixed penalty, directly training the model to commit to and complete an answer rather than loop indefinitely.

Degenerate_output is the mode with the thinnest 'commission a labeled dataset' story in this report. Its two concrete, evidenced training levers — length-reward RL and end-of-sequence-penalty reward shaping — are reward-function edits layered on top of existing verifiable-reward data, not new annotation programs. The one genuinely dataset-shaped artifact, variable-length chain-of-thought SFT pairs, is per the survey auto-constructible rather than requiring human raters, meaning a lab likely needs a reward-design engagement more than a data-labeling one, alongside a loop-rate census to scope which model sizes and settings actually need the intervention.

modes.label: Constraint unaddressed (no trace)
modes.description: The answer neither satisfies nor engages the constraint; without a reasoning trace, extraction misses and synthesis drops cannot be told apart.
strategy: This is a measurement artifact of trace-less grading, not a trainable failure mode in its own right: without a reasoning trace, the answer-observable label 'constraint unaddressed' cannot distinguish constraint_never_surfaced (the requirement was never extracted from the prompt) from constraint_dropped (it was tracked internally but lost before the final answer) — those are the two trainable modes this bucket collapses. No dataset should be commissioned directly against this key; instead, the coarse signal should be used to prioritize rerunning the same prompts with reasoning enabled, which reclassifies each case into constraint_never_surfaced or constraint_dropped, whichever of this report's two commissionable dossiers then applies.

modes.label: Judge suspect
modes.description: You cannot independently locate the asserted failure: reading the response (and trace, if present) the criterion appears satisfied. Use this instead of inventing a root cause.
strategy: This key marks a disagreement between the grading judge and the failure analyst, not a model training failure — the analyst re-reads the response, and trace if present, and cannot independently locate the criterion violation the judge asserted. No training dataset maps to it because there is no confirmed model behavior to target: the taxonomy's own training implication for this key is 'None.' Its function is diagnostic — cases tagged here feed a human-validation priority queue to check whether the judge itself erred, not a corpus to commission.

modes.label: Other
modes.description: A real failure that fits none of the categories above. Describe it precisely in `rationale`.
strategy: This is a real failure that fits none of the eight derived categories, captured with a precise free-text rationale rather than forced into an ill-fitting bucket. No dataset can be commissioned against an unclassified catch-all: per the taxonomy's own training implication, a rising rate in this key is itself the signal that the taxonomy needs revision — a new derived category should be split out and given its own strategy and dataset dossier — not that training data should be bought against 'other' as it currently stands.
